title: When Detention Is a Revenue Line
hook: Contract out a coercive government function and you create a company whose earnings rise with enforcement — and whose shareholders now have a stake in how the policy goes.
key_points: CoreCivic and GEO Group reported a combined $1.4 billion in quarterly revenue for April–June 2026.
CoreCivic's revenue rose over 27% year over year to $684.9 million; GEO Group's rose about 15% to $732.1 million.
CoreCivic also booked $1.6 billion in net proceeds selling four facilities to DHS — an average of $307,000 per bed — while continuing to operate them.
US immigration detention held almost 66,000 people, per the nonpartisan TRAC, against a stated goal of 100,000 beds.
Supervision is a second revenue stream: ankle monitors, smartwatches and an app under GEO's ISAP contract, plus transportation and deportation flights.
The revolving door runs both ways — a former GEO executive is acting ICE director, and the border czar previously consulted for the company.
content_html: Governments outsource plenty of things without much controversy: building roads, running cafeterias, writing software. Detention is different, because it is the state exercising force, and because the contractor's income depends on how much of it there is. NPR's reporting on the latest quarterly earnings of the two largest US private prison companies shows what that looks like on an income statement.
extra_html:
CoreCivic and GEO Group together reported about $1.4 billion in revenue for April through June 2026. CoreCivic's total rose just over 27% year over year to $684.9 million, which its chief executive attributed partly to more people in detention and partly to lower operating costs — the business of detaining people getting cheaper. GEO Group's revenue climbed roughly 15%, up nearly $96 million, to $732.1 million. Separately, CoreCivic booked $1.6 billion in net proceeds from selling four facilities to the Department of Homeland Security at an average of $307,000 per bed, and will keep operating them under contract. The demand side: nearly 66,000 people were in immigration detention according to the nonpartisan Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, close to record levels, against a stated administration goal of 100,000 at once.

Two features generalize beyond this industry. The first is that outsourcing creates an interest group. Executives on those earnings calls discussed growth in electronic supervision — ankle monitors, smartwatches and the SmartLink app under GEO's Intensive Supervision Appearance Program contract — and GEO's chief executive told investors that the end of Temporary Protected Status for Haitian immigrants should push more people into monitoring; transportation and deportation flight revenue rose with removals. A company positioned that way profits whether enforcement means detention or supervision. The second is the revolving door: a former GEO executive, David Venturella, is acting director of ICE and has told lawmakers he divested his stock; the border czar was a paid GEO consultant before joining the government; a former attorney general lobbied for the company. NPR also cites a Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics analysis finding 29 trades of private prison stocks by the president's brokers since his return to office, totaling in the hundreds of thousands of dollars. None of that is unique to immigration — it is the standard accountability problem whenever a public function acquires private shareholders.

related.title: When Detention Conditions Become a Pressure Tactic
related.hook: Immigration detention is supposed to hold people while their case is decided — not persuade them to give up on it. Reporting from inside a Texas facility raises exactly that question.

related.hook: Public schools face extensive state regulation. Private schools funded by the same taxpayer dollars, through vouchers, often don't — a gap one Arkansas case exposed starkly.

related.title: Regulatory Capture
related.hook: Who protects a city's drinking water when the industry that put it at risk is also the one the regulator was built to serve? That's the problem political scientists call regulatory capture.

related.title: Interest Groups & Lobbying
related.hook: Between elections, organized groups press their case to government every day. Lobbying is how that pressure is applied — and it's both a feature and a worry of democracy.

flashcards.prompt: What incentive does contracting out detention create that direct government operation does not?
flashcards.back_html: A private operator's revenue rises with the number of people detained, so it gains a financial interest in the enforcement policy itself — and the standing of a lobbying interest.

flashcards.prompt: How do these companies earn money when people are released rather than detained?

choices.text: Through electronic supervision contracts — ankle monitors, smartwatches and phone apps
They earn nothing outside of detention beds
Through fines paid directly by released individuals

flashcards.explanation_html: GEO's ISAP contract covers monitoring outside detention; executives told investors that ankle monitoring should grow as more people become subject to enforcement. The app costs far less than the monitors.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the movement of executives between the companies and government draw scrutiny?

choices.text: Officials who write and enforce detention policy have prior financial ties to the firms it enriches
Federal law forbids anyone from ever working in both sectors
It means the companies are formally part of the government

flashcards.explanation_html: A former GEO executive is acting ICE director (he says he divested his stock) and the border czar previously consulted for the company — the classic revolving-door concern about captured judgment.
